Perfect competition is an idealized market structure in economic theory where many buyers and sellers trade homogeneous goods, all have perfect information, and entry and exit are costless. Though rarely if ever seen in reality, perfect competition is the benchmark against which actual markets are measured and the foundation for much microeconomic analysis. Perfect competition requires many small firms with no single firm able to influence price, identical products, perfect information, free entry and exit, and perfectly elastic factor supplies. In perfect competition, price equals marginal cost, firms earn zero economic profit in long-run equilibrium, and allocative efficiency holds—no resources are wasted. Firms are price-takers, not price-makers; they cannot set prices but can only choose quantity to supply at the market-determined price. Adam Smith's concept of the invisible hand—the idea that self-interest channels individual actions toward the common good—presupposes something like perfect competition. Real markets depart from perfect competition because of barriers to entry, product differentiation, and information asymmetries. Markets in monopoly, oligopoly, or monopolistic competition exhibit these departures. Perfectly competitive outcomes are Pareto efficient—no reallocation can make someone better off without harming another—making the model a yardstick for policy evaluation. David Ricardo built comparative advantage theory on a foundation of competitive markets. Alfred Marshall formalized the mathematical model of perfectly competitive equilibrium.
